newsitem.title: USA: Silicon Valley startup to pay online users for time.
newsitem.headline: Silicon Valley startup to pay online users for time.

text.p: A small Silicon Valley startup company with some hefty financial backers is launching an online service that will pay consumers for their time, while providing them with information aimed at their interests.

The Menlo Park, Calif.-based company, called PowerAgent, is not the first company to offer to pay consumers to read advertising and commercial offers, but it hopes to improve upon a concept pioneered by another startup CyberGold.
"We become an agent for consumers," said David Carlick, network president, PowerAgent. "It's better than free."
PowerAgent represents clients online and when customers register, they specify the kinds of information they want to receive, for example, buying a car or travel discounts.

Then PowerAgent matches personal profiles with offers and messages, based on a customer request. Beginning in the fall, it will deliver the information in the way the user prefers, whether it is via e-mail, a frame delivered to a small section of a desktop, or in full screen messages that pop up in the browser, while waiting for Web sites to load.

There is no charge to use PowerAgent and the company does not sell profiles of its users. Carlick said that PowerAgent has a third party which actually stores the names and the e-mail addresses of its customers, while PowerAgent just retains the profiles.

"Some of your information is on one server, and the other server (that is maintained by a third party) has your name, etc.," Carlick said. Increasingly, Internet users are becoming more and more concerned and annoyed by the junk e-mail they receive based on data companies have collected on them.
PowerAgent said that between 25 to 40 percent of the fees it collects from its marketed are passed onto its consumers.

"Our service is based around a bill of rights to consumers," Carlick said, adding that a consumer's profile is a valuable asset and consumer should be compensated for letting marketers have access to it.

PowerAgent was founded in 1994 and currently has about $17 million in venture funding, with investors including Electronic Data Systems, St. Paul Venture Capital, Information Technology Ventures and Fayez Sarofim & Co.
Initial advertisers are Nations Bank, Creative Media LLC, Lpage, DraftDirect Worldwide and i-traffic.

Analysts said that while this type of Internet-based business has the potential to be incredibly lucrative, in order for this concept to work, PowerAgent needs to get millions of members, and lots of advertisers with all kinds of information and services.

"It's like having someone do your personal shopping," said Bill Bass, a Forrester Research analyst. "PowerAgent could actually take off if they have a big enough database of people that make it worth a marketer's time to develop things for PowerAgent." But he added PowerAgent could be a spectacular success, or a spectacular failure. "I don't think it ends up in the middle," Bass said.
Users can register for PowerAgent for free starting Monday, Aug. 4, at http://www.poweragent.com. PowerMail, PowerFrames and PowerPages will be available in October.

Nat Goldhaber, the founder, chairman and CEO of Berkeley, Calif.-based CyberGold, said that PowerAgent's entry into the market endorses his company's business, adding that his firm is only four months old, with 20 advertisers and 20 more in final negotiations.
"It is a valid concept that people's attention is valuable and they should be compensated for it," Goldhaber said. "Welcome on board PowerAgent and may the best company win."
